The post UK startup Pharosyn raises €2.5 million for pharma competitive intelligence platform appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
London-based Pharosyn, which builds AI infrastructure for commercial decision-making in pharma, has raised €2.5 million to expand its platform and support wider adoption across pharmaceutical commercial and portfolio strategy teams.

The round was led by Moonfire, including investments from Entrepreneurs First, Transpose Platform and General Advance.

“Today, I am pretty proud of our product but the scope for improvement is huge. I know I will look back on it in 6 months and be almost embarrassed – the same way that I look back on earlier in the year – that’s the joy of building super quickly as the tech changes constantly all around us,” said co-founder Joshua Hampson in a public statement.

Pharosyn’s raise sits amid notable 2026 investment in AI and data infrastructure serving pharmaceutical and biotech teams.

EU-Startups has reported approximately €75.3 million across seven comparable or adjacent rounds this year, including London-based Sable Bio’s €3.15 million Seed round for AI-powered drug-safety intelligence and Helical’s €8.4 million Seed round for its virtual AI lab for pharma R&D, providing two same-country comparisons.

Other financings include Rivia’s €13 million Series A for clinical-trial data infrastructure and Biorce’s €43.8 million Series A for AI-driven clinical trials.

Mattias Ljungman, founder of Moonfire, says: “Pharosyn’s founders are deeply technical, exceptionally tenacious and ambitious, and determined to be best-in-class globally. They are rare founders who clearly stand out. We could not be more excited to lead this round.”

Founded in 2025, Pharosyn is an AI-powered competitive intelligence platform built for biopharma. Their offering monitors clinical, regulatory, and commercial data sources to produce strategic reports tailored to an organisation’s pipeline.

Pharosyn was founded by Stephen Cowley and Joshua Hampson, who brought Cambridge University backgrounds in AI research and biochemistry. The team also features engineering experience in deploying AI in financial forecasting and enterprise productivity, alongside decades of senior executive experience consulting in pharmaceutical commercial strategy at Citeline and leading consulting firms.

Pharosyn is built on two convictions: that pharmaceutical companies need custom AI infrastructure to maintain a competitive advantage, and that embedding this infrastructure deep inside pharma teams can improve commercial decision-making.

By increasing the depth of insight, scope of analysis and speed at which teams can work, Pharosyn looks to help companies make better decisions about where to allocate resources. Its infrastructure can be deployed across commercial strategy, portfolio strategy, business development & licensing, market research, forecasting and competitive intelligence.

Today, senior directors at top-10 pharmaceutical companies reportedly use Pharosyn to inform their strategic decisions.

The post UK startup Pharosyn raises €2.5 million for pharma competitive intelligence platform appeared first on EU-Startups.

item.title: MIRAVA raises €4.2 million to build a new category in recreational boating (Sponsored)
item.dc:creator: Ethan Conroy
item.description:
MIRAVA, a smart recreational boat startup, has raised €4.2 million ($5 million) in angel funding to move from three years of product development into small-batch production and customer deliveries. The company has spent the past three years developing its first product, combining intelligent navigation, a modular design and software-driven experiences into a single recreational boat […]

The post MIRAVA raises €4.2 million to build a new category in recreational boating (Sponsored) appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
MIRAVA, a smart recreational boat startup, has raised €4.2 million ($5 million) in angel funding to move from three years of product development into small-batch production and customer deliveries.

The company has spent the past three years developing its first product, combining intelligent navigation, a modular design and software-driven experiences into a single recreational boat platform.

MIRAVA will introduce the product to the European market at the Cannes Yachting Festival in September 2026, followed by boot Düsseldorf in January 2027.

A traditional market ready for a different approach

Recreational boating remains a highly established industry, with many products still organised around traditional use cases such as cruising, fishing, water-sports and entertaining.

At the same time, consumers in other industries have become accustomed to products that are connected, adaptable and increasingly assisted by software and intelligent technologies.

MIRAVA believes recreational boating can undergo a similar transition.

Instead of developing another boat around a single activity, the company has spent three years developing a platform designed to adapt to different ways of spending time on the water.

The idea is straightforward: the boat should adapt to the user, rather than the user having to adapt to the boat.

Building the product around real-world use

MIRAVA’s first smart boat is designed for multiple experiences, including cruising, family leisure, socialising, swimming, fishing and water-sports.

Its modular stern is central to this approach. The aft section can be transformed to create different configurations depending on the activity, while the detachable section can operate independently as a tender or water platform.

This means that the same boat can move between different uses without being defined by a single purpose.

For MIRAVA, this is an opportunity to develop a broader category of intelligent recreational boats – products that combine the flexibility of a multi-purpose platform with the convenience of intelligent technology.

Technology designed around the user.

The company is also taking a different approach to marine technology.

Rather than treating autonomous systems as features that exist primarily to demonstrate technical capability, MIRAVA is applying them to practical boating scenarios.

Its intelligent navigation system includes autonomous docking, autonomous departure and arrival, Dynamic Positioning and intelligent following.

A smart wearable allows users to interact with the boat and can enable it to follow a swimmer, paddle-boarder or diver at a safe distance.

The objective is to reduce some of the complexity involved in operating a boat, allowing users to spend more time on the experience itself.

In this sense, MIRAVA sees intelligent technology as an enabler of freedom rather than an end in itself.

From product development to commercialisation.

The $5M angel investment marks an important stage in MIRAVA’s development.

After three years focused on product development and refinement, the company is now preparing to move towards small-batch production and customer deliveries.

The funding will be used to continue developing the product and its intelligent systems while supporting the next stage of manufacturing and delivery.

This transition also gives MIRAVA an opportunity to test its new approach with customers and the wider European boating market.

The company will use its appearance at Cannes and Düsseldorf to introduce the product to potential customers, partners and the wider marine industry.

A new category, rather than another boat

MIRAVA’s ambition is not simply to add autonomous technology or electric propulsion to an existing boat category.

The company is attempting to combine several trends – intelligent navigation, modular product design, connected interaction and multi-purpose leisure – into a single ownership experience.

The result is a smart boat that can support different activities without being defined by any one of them.

For a market where product categories have traditionally been shaped around specific activities, MIRAVA believes this creates room for a different proposition: a recreational boat designed around how people want to use it, rather than what the boat was originally built to do.

With its initial three years of development complete and new funding secured, MIRAVA is now entering the next phase of its journey – moving from product development towards production, customer delivery and international market introduction.

Its European debut at Cannes will be the first major step in bringing that proposition to market.

item.title: From the frontline: Ukraine’s cyber security learnings for EU founders
item.dc:creator: Iryna Volnytska
item.description:
In December 2015, Russian hackers managed to cut electricity for about 225,000 customers across three Ukrainian regions. They had been inside those networks for months, and nobody had noticed. By 2024, Ukraine faced 4,315 registered incidents in a single year, with 59 of them labelled as critical. The previous year saw 2,543 attacks, with 364 […]

The post From the frontline: Ukraine’s cyber security learnings for EU founders appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
In December 2015, Russian hackers managed to cut electricity for about 225,000 customers across three Ukrainian regions. They had been inside those networks for months, and nobody had noticed.

By 2024, Ukraine faced 4,315 registered incidents in a single year, with 59 of them labelled as critical. The previous year saw 2,543 attacks, with 364 considered serious. The number of incidents grew, but the impact was much smaller.

Four years of those incidents are collected in “Four Years on the Digital Frontline“, a report by IronCyber and SET University. Ukraine’s experience led to three core habits: understanding what’s already inside your systems, learning from incidents that have already happened, and keeping operations running when something goes wrong.

Here’s how these lessons apply to European companies.

Someone can hold your systems for months before anything shows

Attackers held access inside Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest mobile operator, for at least seven months before the takedown. The visible part lasted one day, in December 2023, and cut service to roughly 24 million people.

The attackers didn’t use sophisticated tricks to gain access. By late 2023, about 40% of registered incidents in Ukraine involved extortion or theft of funds. Attackers leaned on whatever got them in first: compromised credentials, exposed edge devices, or brokers selling access someone else had already taken. 

Even your own software can be a target. In September 2024, Russian hackers distributed malware via Signal, disguised as a military app called GRISELDA. They also sent files that created secret connections back to their systems, all packaged as routine admin emails. Neither attack exploited a product flaw, they relied on the trust users already had in those tools.

Before your next board meeting, know two things: how many of your systems are accessible from the internet, and how long it would take you to spot an outsider using valid credentials. If you can’t answer the second, make it your top priority – investors and potential buyers will ask the same question.

Every incident, even an unfinished one, became a procedure

Ukrainian cybersecurity progress between 2015 and 2024 wasn’t only about getting better tools. Ukrainian teams treated every incident as material. Each one was taken apart, and what came out went into the procedures, the detection rules and the hardening. The same attack met a prepared system the second time.

A phishing chain that landed in March shaped how the next one was handled in April. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, serious incidents dropped from 364 to 59, which the report puts down to a working cycle of adaptation.

Unfinished attacker work is worth studying too. In 2023, defenders found malware built to send commands to grid substation equipment. It could not run reliably yet, which meant someone was still testing. For anyone who trained against that sample, it was months of warning.

Many national cyber response teams publish the raw material for free. Pick three recent incidents from your sector, write up what happened and walk your team through it

Build the version that still works when the main thing breaks

Ukrainian power engineers avoided total blackouts by going old-school: they isolated sections manually, rerouted power, and used mechanical overrides when control systems failed. With ransomware, having tested backups is still the only sure way to keep things running without giving in to demands.

Drone teams adapted too. When radio and satellite links were jammed, they switched to fibre-optic tethers, then developed optical navigation to keep drones on mission even if GPS was knocked out.

Staying resilient isn’t just about technology. In Ukraine, stolen documents and technical drawings were published deliberately, as pressure. Separately, by 2025 attackers were using AI to work through exfiltrated material and compromised mailboxes at speed, picking out what was worth having. Sorting through a hacked inbox is now cheap and fast for cybercriminals.

So, make sure you have backups you’ve actually restored from, a way for your product to run without its most critical dependency, and have customer communication ready before a crisis hits.

Protect what a competitor would want, not what customers can see

Everything above covers disruption. None of it covers the attack where nothing happens.

In 2024, Russian hackers targeted Ukrainian defence manufacturers for their design data (including sensitive data on weapons and protection technology). There was no ransom demand, no encryption, no visible outage. The damage is deferred. What was taken sits in someone else’s research programme, and you have no way to know it happened.

Many founders lock down their production systems, but leave design files, training data, and test results on shared drives with open access. Do the opposite: lock down sensitive development data and log every access.

Where to start

None of this is theoretical. The substations went dark. The mobile network went down for 24 million people. The malware was found, named and published. And the methods are not confined to Ukraine. Microsoft’s 2025 Digital Defense Report found the 10 countries most affected by Russian cyber activity outside Ukraine were all NATO members, a 25% increase year on year. 

Four things are worth doing, and none needs a budget. Write up every incident you handle, including the near misses, and keep those write-ups somewhere engineers actually read them. Benchmark against published reports from other companies in your sector, not against your own last quarter. And when someone makes a call under pressure that turns out wrong, record how the decision was made, not just what the outcome was.

Map what you depend on, not only what you own. Shared suppliers, update channels, satellite links and service providers are how someone else’s incident becomes yours. This is the part almost nobody does thoroughly.

The post From the frontline: Ukraine’s cyber security learnings for EU founders appeared first on EU-Startups.

item.title: British Business Bank commits €53.6 million to Zinc’s €81.5 million Science-for-Impact Fund
item.dc:creator: Rahul Raj
item.description:
The British Business Bank has agreed to commit up to €53.6 million (£46 million) to Zinc Capital Management‘s second institutional fund, the Science-for-Impact Fund.  The commitment was made through the Enterprise Capital Funds programme. It will support Zinc’s Science-for-Impact investment strategy, which backs entrepreneurs from the earliest stages of company creation and helps transform scientific […]

The post British Business Bank commits €53.6 million to Zinc’s €81.5 million Science-for-Impact Fund appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
The British Business Bank has agreed to commit up to €53.6 million (£46 million) to Zinc Capital Management‘s second institutional fund, the Science-for-Impact Fund. 

The commitment was made through the Enterprise Capital Funds programme. It will support Zinc’s Science-for-Impact investment strategy, which backs entrepreneurs from the earliest stages of company creation and helps transform scientific breakthrough ideas across the UK into scalable businesses. The investment follows the Bank’s 2022 commitment to Zinc II and will enable Zinc to expand its support for founders.

Mark Sims, Managing Director, Head of Development Equity Funds, British Business Bank, said, “Breakthrough businesses need support from the very earliest stages if they’re to realise their potential. Zinc has a strong track record of backing founders tackling significant health and environmental challenges, and we’re pleased to support the next phase of its growth. Our commitment to Zinc will help strengthen the pipeline of innovative businesses driving the UK’s future economy.”

Founded in 2017, Zinc is a pre-Seed venture capital firm backing ambitious founders building Science-for-Impact companies in health and the environment. It states that it invests at the earliest stages and partners with “exceptional teams” right across the UK, developing breakthrough science and deep technologies with the potential to create category-defining businesses.

Zinc helps founders de-risk scientific innovation, accelerate commercial progress, and build companies that deliver both significant societal impact and long-term value creation through a combination of first-cheque investment and specialist venture-building support. 

Its portfolio includes SignaCor (first-in-class therapeutics for heart disease), Epiome (an AI-powered biomarker platform for neurodegenerative diseases), Speek (a digital clinical care platform for teenage self-harm), Spine (an AI operating system for grid-scale battery asset management), and CellMine (a waste-free process to recycle lithium-ion batteries).

Zinc’s Science-for-Impact Fund is targeting a €81.5 million (£70 million) fund size and aims to build a portfolio of 80 new DeepTech companies. The VC firm notes that the fund’s strategy aligns closely with the government’s industrial strategy priorities across advanced manufacturing, clean energy, life sciences, as well as engineering, biology and AI.

Ella Goldner, co-founder and Managing Partner, Zinc, said, “The UK is home to some of the world’s most extraordinary scientific talent, yet too many breakthrough discoveries never become the companies that improve lives, protect our planet and create long-term economic value. 

“We founded Zinc to change that by partnering with exceptional scientists and entrepreneurs across the UK at the earliest stages, helping transform world-class research into ventures that deliver lasting impact in health and the environment while building the globally significant businesses of the future. We are proud to continue our partnership with the British Business Bank, whose long-standing support reflects a shared conviction that backing ambitious founders early is one of the most powerful ways to strengthen the UK’s innovation economy.”

With this commitment, the British Business Bank aims to help accelerate the creation and growth of innovative UK DeepTech startups tackling critical health and environmental challenges. 

As the largest investor in UK venture and venture growth capital funds, the British Business Bank states that it regularly makes cornerstone commitments, enabling funds to achieve a first close and helping them execute their planned strategy more effectively and often at greater scale.

The Bank’s Enterprise Capital Funds programme aims to increase the supply of equity capital to early-stage UK companies with long-term growth potential. It also lowers barriers to entry for fund managers looking to operate in the VC market by providing a return structure that makes it more attractive to private-sector investors.

Misodzi Mukungurutse, Senior Investment Manager, Development Equity Funds, British Business Bank, said, “What sets Zinc apart is its ability to work closely with founders from day one, helping turn promising ideas into investable businesses. That hands-on approach, combined with a clear Science-for-Impact strategy, positions the fund well to support the UK’s next generation of innovative startups.”

The post British Business Bank commits €53.6 million to Zinc’s €81.5 million Science-for-Impact Fund appeared first on EU-Startups.

item.title: Adressing complicated pregnancies, iPremom raises €15 million to advance early detection
item.dc:creator: David Cendon Garcia
item.description:
iPremom, a Spanish molecular diagnostics company addressing the early identification of pregnancy complications, has raised €15 million in Seed funding to support clinical validation and the commercial rollout of its MaiRa platform, which analyses early signals of first-trimester pregnancy complications through blood tests. The round was led by Amadeus Capital Partners, with participation from Asabys […]

The post Adressing complicated pregnancies, iPremom raises €15 million to advance early detection appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
iPremom, a Spanish molecular diagnostics company addressing the early identification of pregnancy complications, has raised €15 million in Seed funding to support clinical validation and the commercial rollout of its MaiRa platform, which analyses early signals of first-trimester pregnancy complications through blood tests.

The round was led by Amadeus Capital Partners, with participation from Asabys Partners and APEX Ventures.

Professor Carlos Simón, co-founder and Chairman of iPremom, says: “Pregnancy complications have been under-diagnosed and under-treated for generations, because the field was looking in the wrong place at the wrong time. Our ambition is not just to build a better preeclampsia test, it is to give every pregnant woman a comprehensive, early molecular picture of her pregnancy. This funding is a critical step toward making that a clinical reality.”

iPremom’s Seed round comes amid a relatively busy European investment flow in molecular diagnostics, women’s health and earlier disease detection in 2026.

EU-Startups has reported approximately €35.8 million across a selected group of adjacent financings this year, including €5 million for Paris-based En Carta Diagnostics’ at-home molecular testing platform, €1.1 million for Germany’s Intu Diagnostics, whose first application focuses on HPV testing in women’s health, €1.7 million for Zurich-based KOVE Medical to reduce preterm-birth risks following foetal surgery, and €5.2 million for menstrual-health company DITTO.

AI- and biomarker-led diagnostics have also attracted capital, including €2.8 million for Moonlight AI and €17.1 million for preventive-health platform Lucis.

In Spain, Barcelona-based Health Lean Analytics has raised more than €2.1 million for hospital-focused HealthTech – marking the closest peer in Spain for iPremom.

Pierre Socha, Partner at Amadeus Capital Partners, adds: “We are delighted to partner again with Prof. Simón, after the success of Igenomix which transformed IVF genetics. iPremom is poised to do the same for prenatal care, an even larger market opportunity. By predicting risk from the first weeks of pregnancy based on a simple blood test, it will inform and prepare millions of expecting couples, arm clinicians with unparalleled insights for targeted intervention, and give every baby the best possible start in life. We are proud to be leading this round.”

Founded in 2019, iPremom is a MedTech company based in Valencia, Spain dedicated to the early prediction and prevention of pregnancy complications through molecular diagnostics and AI-based predictive models.

iPremom’s MaiRa platform is built on more than a decade of research by co-founders Professor Carlos Simón, MD, PhD, Chairman of iPremom, and Dr. Tamara Garrido, Chief Scientific Officer. Their work shows that the molecular signals linked to pregnancy complications can be detected in maternal blood from the first trimester, well before clinical symptoms appear.

In preeclampsia, for example, this is linked to decidualisation resistance, where the uterine lining does not develop as expected, leaving a detectable cell-free RNA (cfRNA) signal in the blood as early as 9 to 14 weeks into the pregnancy.

Using a single blood sample, clinicians can use MaiRa to analyse cfRNA and use predictive modelling to assess risk across a range of pregnancy complications, such as preeclampsia, months before symptoms appear.

The platform has been developed using real-life patient data from more than 26,000 samples, linked to 10,000 pregnancies that were part of the PREMOM study, one of Spain’s largest prospective clinical trials. This dataset is also already supporting the identification of molecular signals linked to a broader set of complications, which will be added to the platform over time.

According to data provided by the company, pregnancy complications remain a major challenge for families and health systems worldwide, claiming 260,000 maternal lives, nearly 2 million babies stillborn at 28 weeks or more of gestation, and 2.3 million children in the first month of life annually.

Preeclampsia alone now affects 5 to 8% of all pregnancies globally, while pre-term birth, foetal growth restriction, and gestational diabetes place further strain on families and health systems. Despite this, iPremom believes that current diagnostic tools often identify risks only after complications have already begun to develop.

The company is now preparing for further regulatory approvals in the EU and USA.

The post Adressing complicated pregnancies, iPremom raises €15 million to advance early detection appeared first on EU-Startups.

item.title: Oslo-based Pistachio acquires Hugin.io to expand into cybersecurity compliance
item.dc:creator: Rahul Raj
item.description:
Pistachio, an Oslo-based AI-powered human risk platform, today announced its IP acquisition of Hugin.io, a Norwegian cyber-risk management platform that helps growing businesses assess, manage and demonstrate their cybersecurity posture and regulatory compliance. With this acquisition, Pistachio aims to broaden its offering beyond human risk to compliance management, strengthening its proposition for SMBs and mid-market […]

The post Oslo-based Pistachio acquires Hugin.io to expand into cybersecurity compliance appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
Pistachio, an Oslo-based AI-powered human risk platform, today announced its IP acquisition of Hugin.io, a Norwegian cyber-risk management platform that helps growing businesses assess, manage and demonstrate their cybersecurity posture and regulatory compliance.

With this acquisition, Pistachio aims to broaden its offering beyond human risk to compliance management, strengthening its proposition for SMBs and mid-market organisations. The financial terms of this deal were not disclosed. 

Joe Jones, Pistachio CEO and co-founder, said, “Organisations are being asked to meet increasingly complex security requirements, but few have the resources to manage them. We built Pistachio around the idea that effective cybersecurity should not require constant effort from already stretched teams. Bringing Hugin’s technology into the platform is a natural next step, allowing us to extend that approach from human risk into compliance and help more organisations build resilience without adding another layer of complexity.”

Founded in 2023, Pistachio is a cybersecurity company building human risk management solutions for SMB and mid-market organisations. The company states that its platform automates security awareness training and insider threat detection, adapting to each employee’s role and behaviour. 

In 2023, the company announced it had raised €3.25 million in a funding round led by Signals VC. The company currently helps organisations address social engineering and insider threats, two of the biggest human risk factors in cybersecurity. The acquisition of Hugin.io adds compliance management as the next capability on its platform.

Jørgen Færevaag, co-Founder and CEO, Hugin.io, said, “Cybersecurity is one of the most significant challenges for growing businesses. The issue is not simply knowing that requirements exist, but understanding what applies to your organisation, where the gaps are and what needs to be done to address them. Hugin’s technology makes that process simpler and more accessible. With Pistachio, the technology will reach a much larger customer base as part of a broader cybersecurity platform, putting know-how in the hands of those that need it most as they scale.”

The new product is set to officially launch in 2027 and encompasses a suite of capabilities designed to help organisations define, measure, and improve their security posture, along with tools for managing devices and applications. Pistachi notes that with these capabilities, the compliance product helps growing businesses stay continuously secure and audit-ready without the burden of manual certification work.

Once launched, the company will support organisations in meeting standards and regulations including ISO 27001, the international standard for information security management; NIS2, the EU directive strengthening cybersecurity requirements across critical sectors; SOC 2, a framework for demonstrating controls around security and data management; and DORA, the EU regulation establishing cybersecurity and operational resilience requirements for the financial sector.

According to Pistachio, compliance is becoming as much a business imperative as a legal one, especially with legislation such as the UK’s Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act coming into force. Through its new offering, Pistachio’s aim is to automate that burden, helping smaller organisations build cyber resilience without requiring enterprise-level resources.

Headquartered in Oslo, with offices in London and Valencia, Pistachio recently surpassed 1,000 customers, predominantly across Europe.

The post Oslo-based Pistachio acquires Hugin.io to expand into cybersecurity compliance appeared first on EU-Startups.

item.title: Germany’s Uplift Ventures debuts €100 million fund to bridge Europe’s DeepTech financing gap
item.dc:creator: Rahul Raj
item.description:
Uplift Ventures, the Hamburg- and Berlin-based venture platform, has launched its inaugural €100 million venture capital fund to back Europe’s next generation of DeepTech founders. The fund is backed by Jungheinrich, the German intralogistics group that founded Uplift Ventures. It will deploy the €100 million across up to 20 startups and selected DeepTech funds, primarily […]

The post Germany’s Uplift Ventures debuts €100 million fund to bridge Europe’s DeepTech financing gap appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
Uplift Ventures, the Hamburg- and Berlin-based venture platform, has launched its inaugural €100 million venture capital fund to back Europe’s next generation of DeepTech founders.

The fund is backed by Jungheinrich, the German intralogistics group that founded Uplift Ventures. It will deploy the €100 million across up to 20 startups and selected DeepTech funds, primarily in Europe and the US, building what it calls a global network that continues to support founders after the initial investment.

“DeepTech requires patient capital and partners who understand both industrial challenges and entrepreneurial ambition. Uplift Ventures invests in the next generation of industrial leaders, making them an important partner for Jungheinrich, firstly with world class financial returns and with immense value for our 2030+ strategy,” said Dr. Lars Brzoska, CEO, Jungheinrich.

Founded in 2025, Uplift Ventures operates as an independently run venture platform backed by Jungheinrich. It has already built the compliance-automation startup turnus.ai in-house and invested in several European DeepTech funds. 

With Europe being home to legacy industry players such as ABB, Siemens, Schneider Electric, and Rolls-Royce, Uplift Ventures wants to use it as a foundation for a new generation of globally relevant technology companies. 

Uplift Ventures says its €100 million DeepTech fund aims to close one of the biggest financing gaps in the European tech ecosystem: the shortage of capital for ambitious DeepTech companies at the late Seed and Series A stages.

The fund will target four sectors: physical AI, energy, enterprise AI and logistics. The firm plans to take a flexible approach to each deal, acting as a lead, co-lead, or participating investor, depending on what best serves the founders and the round.

To lead the new fund, Christian Noske has joined Uplift Ventures as Founding General Partner, joining a leadership team that already includes Kerk Wichmann, Christina Hammes, and Maike Steding.

Noske brings more than ten years of Deep Tech investing experience, having led European investments at NGP Capital and served as a founding partner at BMW i Ventures and Alliance Ventures. His past backing includes The Exploration Company, ANYbotics, Tekion, Dataloop and WeRide, and he hosts the podcast “DeepTech Unleashed”. 

“We’ve spent years investing in Deep Tech and have seen both the many ways these companies can fail and what it takes to build exceptional outcomes. I’m excited about launching Uplift Ventures’ new fund: Europe needs dedicated Deep Tech investors who are in it for the long run. Founders build great companies—we’re here to have their backs and provide resources, experience and a global perspective,” said Noske.

Noske is joined by an investment team of Katharina Schild, Lukas Böttcher, Susan Suzart and Helge Jelinski, who together have previously worked at firms including Cathay Innovation, Speedinvest, Mimic Robotics and Start Global, and have collectively backed more than 30 startups across various technology sectors.

The firm plans to keep growing its team over the coming months as it makes its first investments in 2026.

The post Germany’s Uplift Ventures debuts €100 million fund to bridge Europe’s DeepTech financing gap appeared first on EU-Startups.

item.title: German SpaceTech HyImpulse secures over €50 million to accelerate Europe’s sovereign launch capabilities
item.dc:creator: Rahul Raj
item.description:
HyImpulse Technologies, a Neuenstadt am Kocher-based manufacturer and system provider of commercial rockets for suborbital and orbital launch services, today announced a Series A Extension round of more than €50 million in equity. The round was co-led by JOIN Capital and Ace Capital Partners, with participation from new investors, including North Ventures, BW-Capital, Bayern Kapital […]

The post German SpaceTech HyImpulse secures over €50 million to accelerate Europe’s sovereign launch capabilities appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
HyImpulse Technologies, a Neuenstadt am Kocher-based manufacturer and system provider of commercial rockets for suborbital and orbital launch services, today announced a Series A Extension round of more than €50 million in equity.

The round was co-led by JOIN Capital and Ace Capital Partners, with participation from new investors, including North Ventures, BW-Capital, Bayern Kapital and the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), alongside continued support from existing shareholders, including Campus Founders Ventures. 

In October 2025, the company announced it had raised €15 million in equity capital as part of its Series A funding round and secured an additional €30 million in financing. The extension round brings the company’s total equity and public funding to more than €125 million.

Dr. Christian Schmierer, co-founder and CEO of HyImpulse, said, “This financing reflects our investors’ confidence in our team, technology and commercial vision. Europe needs sovereign, responsive and economically sustainable launch capabilities. Our proprietary hybrid propulsion technology and suborbital and orbital services position us to meet growing demand across commercial, institutional and defence markets.”

HyImpulse was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) by Dr. Schmierer, Dr. Mario Kobald, Konstantin Tomilin, and Ulrich Fischer. Headquartered in southern Germany, HyImpulse is a launch services company that develops and provides suborbital and orbital launch capabilities based on a proprietary propulsion technology. 

The company’s mission is to open access to space by delivering affordable, reliable launch and in-space services. Its proprietary hybrid propulsion technology combines non-explosive paraffin fuel with liquid oxygen and claims to offer a safe, cost-efficient and scalable alternative to conventional kerosene-based systems. 

The German firm also notes that its lower system complexity and reduced component count enable safer, more responsive launch operations and competitive launch economics. 

HyImpulse already operates a commercial suborbital platform, the suborbital launcher SR75. Following its inaugural flight campaign at the Koonibba Test Range in South Australia in 2024, the company is preparing its next SR75 launch from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland. 

HyImpulse’s SR75 and its broader suborbital roadmap targets offer launch capabilities of up to Mach 15 and ranges of up to 10,000 kilometres. According to the company, this addresses growing demand from government agencies, research organisations and defence customers for hypersonic testing, threat simulation, and suborbital flight services.

The company reports that it is capitalising on growing demand for independent launch capabilities, with an order book exceeding €350 million across its suborbital and orbital programmes. 

“Europe doesn’t just need more rockets; it needs launch economics that actually work. HyImpulse has built a fundamentally leaner rocket architecture: roughly half the parts, a path to half the cost per kilogram and far less capital required to get to orbit. They have already proven the technology in flight. That’s why we co-led this round, and why the upcoming SR75 launch matters,” said JOIN Capital Founding Partner Jan Borgstädt.

The company plans to use this funding to accelerate development and commercialisation of HyImpulse’s launch services portfolio, including the second SR75 launch from SaxaVord Spaceport by the end of 2026 and the maiden flight of its launch vehicle SL1. 

It also intends to expand production capabilities and scale commercial operations across Europe and beyond. It will also strengthen the company’s position in key growth markets, including dedicated and responsive satellite launch services, in-space mobility, and suborbital research and defence applications. It has over 100 employees at locations in Neuenstadt, Ottobrunn and Glasgow.

item.title: The problem in Europe’s DefenceTech bottleneck
item.dc:creator: Jean-François Morizur
item.description:
According to reports, Europe’s weapons factories are expanding at three times the rate they did in peacetime, covering some 7 million square metres of new industrial development. Indeed, around the world, governments are investing a fortune in building the manufacturing capacity for critical technologies […]

The post The problem in Europe’s DefenceTech bottleneck appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
According to reports, Europe’s weapons factories are expanding at three times the rate they did in peacetime, covering some 7 million square metres of new industrial development. This, the report goes on, “represents rearmament on a historic scale”.

Indeed, around the world, governments are investing a fortune in building the manufacturing capacity for critical technologies such as advanced semiconductors. Yet they are making the mistake of assuming that supply chains scale in proportion to manufacturing; in other words, that if they build more factories, the firms supplying those factories will automatically expand at the same rate.

This assumption can spell trouble for DefenceTech startups and scale-ups. A company may raise money, win orders and increase its production capacity, only to find that a single scarce component prevents it from delivering.

The reality is that advanced industries often reach a point where demand for critical parts, materials or skills outstrips supply. A factory may therefore be ready to ramp up production while still waiting months for a specialist chip or component.

Building factories isn’t enough if the parts come from elsewhere or if only one or two companies make them. A whole industrial base must exist to support those factories if they’re to keep producing the final technology at scale.

Not all markets scale in the same way

What might a sound industrial policy look like? That depends on the kind of market involved. Broadly, there are at least three categories.

In mature industries, companies represent only a tiny share of an established market, and supply chains naturally absorb additional demand. Suppliers already serve many customers and production methods are well understood. Standard mechanical parts are a good example.

In developing markets, supply can expand alongside manufacturers, but only if there is coordination and certainty about the future. Governments may need to coordinate orders or make long-term commitments so that suppliers can justify investing.

In emerging strategic technology markets, companies are scaling the market rather than scaling within it. SpaceX is one such example. Many DefenceTech startups and scale-ups face this problem, only on a smaller scale.

A fast-growing manufacturer can demand parts in quantities that the wider market has never had to supply. There may be few alternative vendors and little spare capacity. In practice, the ability to scale rests not only on the quality of the technology involved or the size of the order book, but on whether the supply base can grow with the company.

This poses a different kind of challenge, one that requires policymakers to think hard about the suppliers that feed the factories.

The missing supplier base

The problem at the moment is that many governments continue to see every manufacturing project as though it belongs to the second category. They assume that, given enough orders, suppliers will expand alongside the main manufacturer.

But many critical defence industries, including advanced semiconductors, quantum technologies and other emerging systems, belong to the third category. The market either does not yet exist or certainly does not exist at the scale at which demand and supply can increase together.

Suppliers may lack the capital, equipment or confidence to expand before demand is guaranteed. Promising scale-ups then find themselves caught between high customer demand and inadequate industrial supply.

This is why governments need to think about how supplier capacity, manufacturing know-how, dual-sourcing and industrial resilience can develop side by side with raw production capacity. That may mean supporting second suppliers, funding shared facilities or placing longer-term orders. It may also mean tailoring procurement and financing schemes to the needs of young companies whose suppliers cannot yet afford to expand.

Resilience is component-specific

Moreover, policymakers need to stop thinking of “the supply chain” as though it were a single entity. This is too simple. Every advanced system is made up of components at different stages of industrial maturity.

An advanced sensor system, for instance, might combine standard mechanical parts sourced from mature global markets, specialist electronic equipment produced by a small supplier base and highly specialised components that belong to an emerging market.

Each of these three classes of components requires a different approach to sourcing and poses different obstacles to scaling. Standard parts may be easy to replace; specialist equipment may come from only a handful of companies; emerging components may have no real substitute at all.

The right policy has to be component-specific. Governments should work out which components can be bought freely, which require long-term coordination and which need an industrial base to be created almost from nothing.

Startups, scale-ups and their investors need to do something similar, since the weakest link in the supply chain can be the deciding factor in whether a company can turn a successful prototype into something that can be mass-produced.

Here is the dilemma: Europe is building more weapons factories, but factories alone don’t guarantee more weapons. A factory can only produce as fast as its suppliers can provide chips, machinery, materials, components and skilled workers.

Therefore, rather than gauging industrial success by the number of factories built or due to be built, governments should ask the far more difficult question of whether the supply base behind those factories can support sustained production, including during a crisis.

This should, at least to some extent, shape how Europe thinks about its DefenceTech companies. A startup is not scalable just because demand for its products exists, or because money is available.

It is scalable only if the suppliers, skills and know-how that enable it to do what it does can develop too.

These invisible networks are becoming one of the main constraints on defence-industrial growth. Until governments understand this distinction, new factories may create the appearance of resilience when, in fact, resilience is still some way off.

item.title: Want to switch to European tech? Start with these 8 websites
item.dc:creator: David Cendon Garcia
item.description:

While researching those lists, one thing quickly became […]

The post Want to switch to European tech? Start with these 8 websites appeared first on EU-Startups.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past month, we have been doing quite a bit of digging into European alternatives to US technology. First, we looked at 10 work-related US tools you can replace right now with European alternatives, before turning to the consumer side with European alternatives for everything else.

While researching those lists, one thing quickly became clear: we were hardly the first people to start compiling alternatives. There are already substantial directories, maps, catalogues and community projects bringing together European software and services, in some cases with thousands of options to browse.

So rather than picking individual replacements, here are 8 websites that can help you do the digging yourself.

Digital-EU

Digital-EU is a non-commercial catalogue dedicated to digital solutions designed and operated by European companies. The interface is deliberately straightforward: users can search for services or browse through categories to identify potential replacements.

The project describes its catalogue as non-exhaustive and regularly updated, with the site showing its latest update as June 2026. For readers who want something closer to a searchable directory without an accompanying manifesto or lengthy policy material, it is one of the simpler places to begin.

European Alternatives

European Alternatives does pretty much what its name promises, concentrating on European replacements for digital services and products such as SaaS platforms and cloud tools. Its database can be explored by category, covering areas including file hosting, object storage, translation, navigation, monitoring and other everyday digital services.

Users can also suggest new products or propose changes, giving the directory a community element alongside its existing catalogue.

European Tech Map

European Tech Map is one of the larger databases on this list. At the time of writing, it says it includes 3,131 companies across 39 categories and 43 countries, with a focus on sovereign and EU-hosted software and services. Categories range from cloud computing, AI and cybersecurity to productivity, accounting, analytics, e-commerce and marketing automation.

Alongside browsing the database itself, users can specifically search for alternatives to US technology or explore companies through an interactive map.

EuroStack Directory

The EuroStack Directory is the catalogue arm of the wider EuroStack push for European digital sovereignty. It currently lists more than 1,700 solutions across 64 categories and seven layers of the digital stack, while mapping alternatives to more than 170 non-European services. That makes it particularly useful if you already know the product you want to replace: the directory groups European options against services including Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, AWS, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Analytics, Mailchimp and HubSpot.

It also allows users to browse by broader layers such as infrastructure, developer tools, security, analytics and productivity.

Go European

Go European describes itself as a community-driven directory for discovering European products and services based on personal recommendations. Listings can be searched and filtered, and individual entries often identify the better-known service they could replace.

That makes it especially accessible for people who are not necessarily thinking in terms of “digital sovereignty”, but simply want to type in a familiar product and see what else exists. Its scope also reaches beyond core enterprise software, making it relevant to both professional and everyday digital habits.

OurSoftware.eu

OurSoftware.eu is another heavyweight option for anyone who wants a large pool of companies to investigate. The directory currently displays more than 3,300 software listings, spread across categories including cloud and hosting, AI, security, productivity, analytics, DevOps, communication, CRM, fintech and document collaboration.

It also builds dedicated alternative pages around familiar products and platforms, including Gmail, Microsoft 365, AWS, Slack, Salesforce and Google Analytics, making it particularly handy when starting with the US service you already use rather than a broad software category.

Switch-to.eu

Switch-to.eu combines a directory with something many databases leave out: the practicalities of actually switching. Its listings cover areas including email, cloud storage, messaging, navigation, search and browsers, while providing information such as where services are based or hosted, their costs and how they handle data.

The volunteer-maintained project also publishes step-by-step migration guides intended to help users move their data from one service to another. That makes it particularly relevant once your research moves from “what are the alternatives?” to “how do I actually leave?”.

Tech Sovereignty Catalogue

The Tech Sovereignty Catalogue takes a more business and infrastructure-oriented approach, presenting European technologies across areas including cloud, AI, cybersecurity, data, applications and industry-specific services.

At the time of writing, the catalogue contains 134 solutions, searchable by company, solution, keyword, category and country, with entries also available through a map view. One caveat is particularly worth noting: submissions are based on information provided by participating companies, and the catalogue itself explicitly advises users to carry out independent due diligence rather than treating inclusion as an endorsement.

The post Want to switch to European tech? Start with these 8 websites appeared first on EU-Startups.
